II. Modeling

Building the model

Target : y Uranium : u.full Floor : x County : county ### Model 0 - Mean We start with a simple model and build up from there. We see that the mean is signifincantly different from 0. We do not accept $ H_0 : = 0 $ \[ y_{i} = \mu + \epsilon_i, \epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2) \]

model_0 <- lm(y ~ 1, df)
anova(model_0)
## Analysis of Variance Table
## 
## Response: y
##            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
## Residuals 918 668.46 0.72817
summary(model_0)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = y ~ 1, data = df)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -3.5272 -0.5828  0.0563  0.5671  2.6507 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)  1.22462    0.02815   43.51   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.8533 on 918 degrees of freedom

Model 1 - Floor

\[ y_{i} = \mu + \alpha_i + \epsilon_i , \quad \epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2) \]

model_1 <- lm(y ~ floor, df)
anova(model_1)
## Analysis of Variance Table
## 
## Response: y
##            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
## floor       1  47.98  47.983  70.914 < 2.2e-16 ***
## Residuals 917 620.47   0.677                      
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Model 2 - Uranium

\[ y_{i} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta x_i+ \epsilon_i , \quad \epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2) \]

model_2 <- lm(y ~ floor + u.full , df)
anova(model_2)
## Analysis of Variance Table
## 
## Response: y
##            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
## floor       1  47.98  47.983  80.489 < 2.2e-16 ***
## u.full      1  74.41  74.412 124.824 < 2.2e-16 ***
## Residuals 916 546.06   0.596                      
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Model 3 - Random effect

\[ y_{i} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta x_i + \gamma_i + \epsilon_i , \quad \epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\epsilon}), \quad \gamma_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\gamma}) \]

model_3 <- lmer(y ~ floor + u.full + (1|county) , df)
ranova(model_3)
## ANOVA-like table for random-effects: Single term deletions
## 
## Model:
## y ~ floor + u.full + (1 | county)
##              npar  logLik    AIC    LRT Df Pr(>Chisq)   
## <none>          5 -1067.1 2144.2                        
## (1 | county)    4 -1071.1 2150.1 7.9559  1   0.004793 **
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
dotplot(ranef(model_3, condVar=TRUE), strip = FALSE, ylab="County") 
## $county

ranef_model_3 <- ranef(model_3, condVar=TRUE)

Model 4 & 5 - Random slopes

We add a random slope to the model to allow the impact of the fixed effects to vary across county.

Random slope for predictor floor By including a random slope for the predictor x, we allow its effect on radon levels to depend on the county. This tests whether counties differ in how strongly basement measurements raise or lower radon levels.

model_4 <- lmer(y ~ x + u.full + (x|county) , df)
ranova(model_4)
## ANOVA-like table for random-effects: Single term deletions
## 
## Model:
## y ~ x + u.full + (x | county)
##                   npar  logLik    AIC    LRT Df Pr(>Chisq)  
## <none>               7 -1064.3 2142.6                       
## x in (x | county)    5 -1067.1 2144.2 5.5459  2    0.06248 .
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

The addition of a random-slope term is not statistically significant (p = 0.062). Therefore, the basement effect appears to be consistent across counties, and the random-intercept model is adequate.

ranef_m4 <- ranef(model_4)$county
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(ranef_m4, aes(x = x, y = `(Intercept)`)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm",
              se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Random Slopes and Intercepts for Counties",
       x = "Slope for floor",
       y = "Intercept") +
#  xlim(-0.6, 0.6) +
#  ylim(-0.4, 0.4) +
  coord_fixed() +   # <-- makes width = height
  theme_minimal()
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

The above graph show the the slopes and intercept for each cluster. We don’t see clear patterns in the points exeot one straight line. I won’t look into further detail as the effect of the random slope are not significant.

Random slope for predictor u.full We skip this since there is no within-county variation.

Full model

\[ y_{i} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta x_i + \gamma_i + \epsilon_i , \quad \epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\epsilon}), \quad \gamma_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\gamma}) \]

model <- lmer(y ~ floor + u.full + (1|county) , df)
summary(model)
## Linear mixed model fit by REML. t-tests use Satterthwaite's method [
## lmerModLmerTest]
## Formula: y ~ floor + u.full + (1 | county)
##    Data: df
## 
## REML criterion at convergence: 2134.2
## 
## Scaled residuals: 
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -4.9673 -0.6117  0.0274  0.6555  3.3848 
## 
## Random effects:
##  Groups   Name        Variance Std.Dev.
##  county   (Intercept) 0.02446  0.1564  
##  Residual             0.57523  0.7584  
## Number of obs: 919, groups:  county, 85
## 
## Fixed effects:
##              Estimate Std. Error        df t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)   1.46576    0.03794  55.34577  38.633  < 2e-16 ***
## floor1       -0.66824    0.06880 902.87114  -9.713  < 2e-16 ***
## u.full        0.72027    0.09176  45.99114   7.849 4.94e-10 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Correlation of Fixed Effects:
##        (Intr) floor1
## floor1 -0.357       
## u.full  0.145 -0.009

\[\hat{\sigma_{\epsilon}} = 0.7584, \quad \hat{\sigma_{\gamma}} = 0.1564 \] We see that only 4 % of the variance is explained by the random effect. \[ \frac{0.024}{0.575 + 0.024} = 4 \% \]

confint(model)
## Computing profile confidence intervals ...
##                   2.5 %     97.5 %
## .sig01       0.05277016  0.2454198
## .sigma       0.72351612  0.7957389
## (Intercept)  1.39137411  1.5415136
## floor1      -0.80224373 -0.5307890
## u.full       0.53732370  0.8992722

Given our observation we are 95% confident that the population mean \(\hat{\mu}\) are between (1.39, 1.54) given floor = 0 and u.full = 0. The slope $ $ are between (0.54, 0.90). And that the effect of floor=1 are between (-08, -0.53)

Comparison

Look at the change to the diagnostic plots as complexity increasses

qqnorm(resid(model_0))
qqline(resid(model_0))

qqnorm(resid(model_3))
qqline(resid(model_3))

Comparison table

AIC(model_0, model_1, model_2, model_3)
##         df      AIC
## model_0  2 2319.479
## model_1  3 2253.025
## model_2  4 2137.621
## model_3  5 2144.186
BIC(model_0, model_1, model_2, model_3)
##         df      BIC
## model_0  2 2329.126
## model_1  3 2267.495
## model_2  4 2156.914
## model_3  5 2168.303
logLik(model_0)
## 'log Lik.' -1157.74 (df=2)
logLik(model_1)
## 'log Lik.' -1123.512 (df=3)
logLik(model_2)
## 'log Lik.' -1064.81 (df=4)
logLik(model_3)
## 'log Lik.' -1067.093 (df=5)
Model df logLik AIC BIC
model_0 2 –1157.740 2319.479 2329.126
model_1 3 –1123.512 2253.025 2267.495
model_2 4 –1064.810 2137.621 2156.914
model_3 5 –1067.093 2144.186 2168.303

We want AIC and BIC to be as small as possible, but it seems that both AIC and BIC is larger for model 2 than 3. \[ \text{AIC} = -2 \log L(\hat{\theta}) + 2p, \] \[ \text{BIC} = -2 \log L(\hat{\theta}) + (\log n)\, p \]

This is partially due to the increase in the complexity penalty since p increases by 1, but we also see an increase in log likelyhood.

Even though the variance of the residuals decrease from \(0.772^2 = 0.596\) in model_2 to \(0.758^2 = 0.575\) in model_3, we get an additional variance from the random effect of \(0.156^2 = 0.024\) meaning that the overall variance increases hich decreasses the log-likeyhood function.

III b) Present a plot of the county level of uranium in the horizontal axis, and the estimated regression intercepts with CI, in the vertical axis. Additionally, one with the estimated regression slopes with CI.

model <- lmer(y ~ floor + u.full + (1|county) , df)

library(lme4)
library(ggplot2)

# Random intercepts with conditional variance
re  <- ranef(model, condVar=TRUE)
u   <- attr(re$county, "postVar")   # 1x1xN array of variances

# Random-intercept estimates
intercepts <- re$county[, "(Intercept)"]

# Std. errors from conditional modes
se <- sqrt(sapply(1:dim(u)[3], function(i) u[,,i]))

# Build dataframe
df_plot <- data.frame(
  county    = rownames(re$county),
  intercept = intercepts,
  lower     = intercepts - 1.96 * se,
  upper     = intercepts + 1.96 * se
)

u_by_county <- aggregate(u.full ~ county, data=df, FUN=unique)
names(u_by_county)[2] <- "u_full_county"

df_plot$u_full <- u_by_county$u_full_county[
  match(df_plot$county, u_by_county$county)
]

ggplot(df_plot, aes(x = u_full, y = intercept)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0) +
  xlab("County-level uranium (u.full)") +
  ylab("Random intercept with 95% CI") +
  ylim(-0.5, 0.5) +
  theme_bw()

# Posterior variance for each county's random intercept
post_var <- sapply(1:dim(u)[3], function(i) u[,,i])

# Build a dataframe with county, variance, SE, and intercept
var_by_county <- data.frame(
  county    = rownames(re$county),
  intercept = re$county[, "(Intercept)"],
  var       = post_var,
  se        = sqrt(post_var)
)

# Counties with the *lowest* conditional variance
var_by_county_lowest <- var_by_county %>% 
  arrange(var)

# View the top few with lowest variance
head(var_by_county_lowest, 10)

library(merTools)
## Loading required package: arm
## 
## arm (Version 1.14-4, built: 2024-4-1)

## 
##     standardize
new_data$floor  <- factor(new_data$floor)
new_data$county <- factor(new_data$county)

pred_ci <- predictInterval(
  model,
  newdata = new_data,
  which   = "full",
  level   = 0.95,
  n.sims  = 1000,
  include.resid.var = TRUE
)
## Warning:      The following levels of county from newdata 
##  -- 100, 101, 102 -- are not in the model data. 
##      Currently, predictions for these values are based only on the 
##  fixed coefficients and the observation-level error.
new_data <- cbind(new_data, pred_ci)
library(lme4)

## Design matrix for the fixed-effects part of the model
## This must match the fixed-effects formula: ~ floor + u.full
X <- model.matrix(~ floor + u.full, data = new_data)

## Fixed-effect estimates and their covariance matrix
beta_hat <- fixef(model)
V_beta   <- vcov(model)

## Standard errors of the linear predictor X * beta
pred_se <- sqrt(diag(X %*% V_beta %*% t(X)))

## 95% confidence intervals
new_data$pred_se  <- pred_se
new_data$lower_ci <- new_data$pred_conditional - 1.96 * pred_se
new_data$upper_ci <- new_data$pred_conditional + 1.96 * pred_se

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(new_data, aes(x = u.full, y = pred_conditional, colour = county)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower_ci, ymax = upper_ci), width = 0) +
  xlab("u.full") +
  ylab("Predicted y (95% CI, fixed effects only)") +
  theme_bw()
